headings: Proposed foundations and their unanswered questions
Skepticism, nihilism and the arguments for them
Two overlapping words and useful distinctions
Two ten-question quizzes with final answer keys
Two sets of fifteen discussion questions
introHeading: Ethics and the demand for moral grounding
intro: The six original prompts and separate ChatGPT and Gemini responses are restored in order. Edited responses distinguish proposed moral foundations from proofs of their authority, clarify skepticism and nihilism, and qualify the distinction between ethics and morality. Both original quizzes and discussion lists follow.
description: Explore ethics, proposed moral foundations, skepticism, nihilism and moral language through six original prompts, revised responses, quizzes and discussion questions.
highlights: Describing a moral practice does not establish its authority.
A criterion for right action is not by itself a proof that moral facts exist.
Ethics and morality overlap in ordinary usage; a chosen distinction must be explained.

replacements.1.1.2: Normative ethics: Examines standards for right action and good character. Utilitarianism assesses overall welfare; deontology emphasizes duties or constraints; virtue ethics examines character and practical judgment. These are proposals to defend, not established answers merely because they have names.
replacements.1.1.5: Ethics asks about duty, virtue and a good life, while also examining whether moral judgments have the authority they claim. For example, describing widespread disapproval of lying is a descriptive task; defending a prohibition is normative; asking what could make the prohibition objectively binding is meta-ethical.
replacements.1.2.2: Normative vs. descriptive: Descriptive inquiry studies existing moral beliefs and practices. Normative inquiry asks which standards should guide action. It need not assume at the outset that those standards are objective moral facts.
replacements.1.2.7: Moral vs. legal: A law can be valid within a legal system yet morally disputed. A moral demand can lack legal recognition. Neither legality nor widespread approval alone settles whether a demand is justified.
replacements.2.1.0: The grounding question asks what, if anything, makes moral claims true or authoritative. The original list mixes proposed foundations, theories of right action and positions about moral truth. Keeping those roles distinct lets us evaluate each proposal without assuming that naming a theory establishes a moral realm.
replacements.2.1.1: Divine command theory: Grounds moral obligation in divine commands. It must explain why those commands bind, how they are identified, and whether goodness depends on command or supplies a reason for it. The existence of a powerful commander alone does not establish moral authority.
replacements.2.1.2: Natural law: Grounds practical principles in an account of human nature and goods. Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II, question 94, explains natural-law precepts through practical reason and human inclinations. A critic can ask how identifying an inclination establishes what ought to be pursued; the theory needs its account of goods, not merely observations of common behavior.
replacements.2.1.3: Deontology: Duty-based theories identify obligations or constraints. Kant connects obligation to rational agency and treats humanity as an end, never merely a means. Distinguish an action’s conformity to duty from its moral worth when done from duty. The further grounding question is why rational agency carries this authority.
replacements.2.1.4: Consequentialism: Evaluates actions through consequences. Utilitarianism takes overall welfare as the relevant standard; Mill’s Utilitarianism, chapter II, explains the happiness criterion. Measuring welfare does not itself establish that maximizing it is obligatory. That normative premise needs a defense.
replacements.2.1.5: Virtue ethics: Examines good character and practical wisdom, often through an account of human flourishing associated with Aristotle. It must explain which traits count as virtues and why its account of flourishing provides a standard for us, rather than simply reflecting admired habits.
replacements.2.1.6: Moral relativism: Makes the truth or justification of moral judgments relative to a framework, rather than establishing framework-independent moral facts. Mere cultural disagreement does not establish relativism, and relativism does not imply that every act is acceptable within every framework.
replacements.2.1.7: Moral realism: Affirms moral truths; stronger formulations emphasize their independence from our attitudes. This states a position to defend, not a complete grounding argument. Realists disagree about what moral facts are and how reason, experience or intuition could give us access to them.
replacements.2.1.8: Constructivism: Explains justified principles through a specified procedure of practical reasoning. Rawls’s construction of principles of justice is one example, not automatically a foundation for every moral claim. The procedure’s starting assumptions and authority require justification; actual agreement alone is insufficient.
replacements.2.1.9: For each proposal ask three questions: What is supposed to ground the claim? How could we know that it does? Why would it bind someone who rejects it? A theory can offer useful guidance while its stronger claim to objective authority remains disputed.
replacements.2.2.0: Attempts to ground morality appeal to divinity, nature, rational insight, agreement or flourishing. Some defend objective facts; others explain moral practice without that commitment. Here are the original approaches, with their different roles made explicit.
replacements.2.2.2: Divine command theory: Makes divine commands constitutive of obligation. The source’s example of Aquinas is better placed under natural law below; a theistic account need not reduce morality to commands.
replacements.2.2.3: Natural law: Appeals to human nature, practical reason and goods. Aquinas is the clearer example here. The challenge is to justify the connection between an account of human nature and binding practical principles.
replacements.2.2.4: Utilitarianism: Uses overall happiness or welfare as a criterion, as in Mill. Its criterion can be combined with different views about moral truth; the label alone does not prove realism.
replacements.2.2.5: Moral intuitionism: Holds that at least some moral principles can be known without inference from other beliefs. This is not simply an innate feeling or permission to trust any impulse. Sidgwick’s examination of intuitive methods distinguishes judgments about particular cases from general principles. His work is a more suitable example here than the original attribution to Hume.
replacements.2.2.6: Social contract approaches: Seek justification through actual or hypothetical agreement under specified conditions. Locke and Rousseau are important political-contract thinkers, but explaining political legitimacy does not automatically ground all moral obligations. Why the proposed agreement should bind remains a central question.
replacements.2.2.8: Objectivity does not mean that a rule admits no exceptions. Likewise, intuitionism does not mean that any personal feeling is authoritative. These approaches need arguments about evidence, scope and justification; describing their appeal does not settle those arguments.
replacements.3.1.0: Moral skepticism questions moral knowledge or justification; some skeptical positions also challenge moral truth. Moral nihilism commonly denies objective moral values. These are distinguishable claims: doubting our access to moral facts is not yet proving that there are none.
replacements.3.1.2: A skeptic may ask what justifies a moral belief and whether the proposed method reliably distinguishes truth from approval. The challenge need not demand certainty: ordinary knowledge is often understood as compatible with possible error. Nor does the absence of direct observation alone refute a moral claim; the issue is whether another adequate justification exists.
replacements.3.1.4: Moral error theory holds that ordinary positive moral judgments purport to attribute properties that nothing possesses. In Mackie’s influential version, the rejected properties are objectively prescriptive values. This does not make every sentence containing moral vocabulary false: a denial of such values can be true on the theory, and reports of people’s beliefs remain possible.
replacements.3.1.7: Evolutionary explanation: If selection shaped a judgment because it aided reproduction rather than because it tracked moral truth, that can challenge our confidence in the judgment. Evolution has no conscious aim. The argument needs to show a relevant disconnect from truth and address possible independent justification; an evolutionary origin alone does not establish falsity.
replacements.3.1.8: Disagreement: Persistent disagreement among informed, reflective people can challenge claims of reliable access to moral truth. A defender can cite mistaken background facts or biased reasoning. The skeptic’s stronger question is whether disagreement persists after such explanations are addressed, not whether disagreement by itself proves there is no truth.
replacements.3.1.9: Queerness: Mackie challenges the idea of values that would inherently prescribe action, and asks how we could know such properties. The objection concerns their claimed authority and our access to them, not merely their invisibility or unfamiliarity. A realist must explain why the proposed properties and way of knowing are credible.
replacements.3.1.10: Subjectivity of experience: Moral reactions often involve emotion and personal perspective. This can support an explanation in terms of attitudes, but does not alone establish that no moral judgment tracks facts. The argument must compare the competing explanations rather than assume its conclusion.
replacements.3.2.2: Core claim: We may lack adequate justification for moral beliefs. Skepticism about knowledge is stronger than the ordinary admission that we can make mistakes, but it need not deny that moral facts exist.
replacements.3.2.4: Disagreement: Divergent judgments raise a question about reliability. They support skepticism only with an argument explaining why error, differing information or bias cannot adequately account for the divergence.
replacements.3.2.5: Emotivism: Offers a different account of moral language: moral utterances express attitudes rather than simply report facts. Expressing disapproval is not the same as reporting “I dislike stealing,” which can itself be true or false. Emotivism is an alternative theory, not by itself a proof of skepticism.
replacements.3.2.7: Core claim: There are no objective moral facts of the proposed kind. This does not deny that pain, preferences, care or social practices are real. Their existence and their alleged objective moral authority are separate questions.
replacements.3.2.9: Moral disagreements: Diversity may support an explanation of moral belief through culture and attitudes. To reach nihilism, one needs a further argument against objective moral facts; disagreement alone is insufficient.
replacements.3.2.10: Evolutionary byproduct: Some moral responses may be explained by selection and social learning without appealing to moral facts. Explaining a belief’s origin can undermine its justification if that origin is insensitive to truth; it does not automatically show that the belief is false.
replacements.4.1.6: In this descriptive use, morality concerns the standards people actually accept and enact. The word also has a normative use: the standards that would be justified, whether or not a community accepts them. State which meaning is intended.
replacements.4.1.9: Universality and context: Neither word guarantees a universal or context-dependent standard. Philosophical ethics includes relativist arguments, while ordinary moral claims can aspire to universal authority. The distinction between the words does not decide that dispute.
replacements.4.1.10: Theory and practice: Calling ethics the study and morality its subject is useful in this discussion. It is a working convention, not a rigid division: applied ethics is practical, and moral reasoning can be highly theoretical.
replacements.4.2.0: The words overlap. One useful contrast is between a person’s convictions and a professional code, but it should not become a definition that makes all morality private and all ethics external.
replacements.4.2.2: Internal compass: Personal morality can refer to an individual’s convictions. Morality can also refer to shared standards or to proposed standards that hold regardless of anyone’s convictions.
replacements.4.2.6: External system: Professional ethics often means a formal code. Ethics also names philosophical inquiry, which can question that code instead of merely enforcing it.
replacements.4.2.7: Focus on action: Applied ethics examines particular practices and cases. The wider field also investigates meaning, justification and character, so it is not confined to applying agreed rules.
replacements.4.2.9: As an analogy, personal convictions resemble a navigator’s habitual route, while a professional code resembles published directions. Philosophical ethics also asks whether either route is defensible. The analogy illustrates two uses; it does not establish that a personal conviction is subjective or a published code authoritative.
replacements.4.2.11: Level: Both words can concern individuals or groups. Specify “personal morality” or “professional ethics” when that contrast is intended.
replacements.4.2.12: Source: Both personal convictions and public codes can arise from custom, religion or reflection. Their origin does not by itself justify them.
replacements.4.2.13: Focus: A useful convention distinguishes the systematic inquiry, ethics, from the standards examined, morality. Ordinary usage often crosses this boundary.
replacements.4.2.19: Use the distinction that serves the conversation, and state it explicitly. Whether a standard is called ethical or moral tells us little about whether it is justified.

replacements.5.1.17: No. Both words can be used in discussions of universal or context-dependent standards.
replacements.5.1.21: Ethics can name systematic inquiry and morality the standards examined. This is a convention: applied ethics is practical, and moral reasoning can be theoretical.
